1.title: the words on the doorpost
1.hook: the little case on the doorframe; what's actually inside it
1.tomorrow: two flames, eighteen minutes before sunset
1.howItsDone: Jews fix a mezuzah, a handwritten parchment of the Shema passages in a case, on the right doorpost of the doorways of the home, and many touch it and kiss their fingertips when passing through.

screen: `DAY ONE.`

segments.voice: That little case on the doorframe. Right side as you walk in, about shoulder height, often tilted. Some people touch it on the way out and kiss their fingertips, as quick as checking for keys. Most people assume the case is the thing. It isn't. The case is just a case. First, a guess: what's inside?
screen: `THE CASE ON THE DOORFRAME.` → `TOUCHED ON THE WAY OUT.` → `WHAT'S INSIDE?`

segments.voice: Inside is a tiny scroll, written by hand on parchment by a trained scribe with a quill. It carries a passage from the Torah that opens with six famous words, the Shema: hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one. The same passage says to write these words on the doorposts of your house. So people did, literally. Mezuzah is simply Hebrew for doorpost: the word for the frame became the word for the scroll. On the back, many scribes write one of God's names, Shaddai, which some read as the initials of guardian of the doors of Israel. Now the tilt. A famous medieval teacher, Rashi, said hang it upright. His grandson said lay it flat. Many Ashkenazi Jews, whose families come from central and eastern Europe, hang it at a slant: a little of both. Many Sephardi Jews hang it upright. And the touch? Not a lucky charm; the great teacher Maimonides warned against treating it as one. It's a reminder. Every time you cross the threshold, going out or coming home, you pass the words.
screen: `A SCROLL, WRITTEN BY HAND.` · `HEAR, O ISRAEL.` · `UPRIGHT OR FLAT? A SLANT.` · `A REMINDER, NOT A CHARM.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Rest your fingertips on the nearest doorframe, or just picture your own front door. Breathe in. As you breathe out, think of one thing you'd like to carry through that door today. Then lift your hand.
The mezuzah. Doorpost, and the handwritten words fixed to it: hear, O Israel. First word on your strand.

segments.voice: Your line: take the words with you. That's what the touch on the way out means. See you tomorrow.

story.text: Soldiers are sent to arrest a Roman nobleman, the emperor's own relative, because he has become a Jew. Twice he talks his captors into joining him, so the emperor sends a third squad with strict orders: don't talk to him. As they lead him out of his house, he puts his hand on the mezuzah. They can't help asking what it is. A human king sits inside while his guards stand outside, he says; here, the people sit inside, and God keeps watch from outside.

2.title: two flames, eighteen minutes before sunset
2.hook: Friday afternoon, a match, two flames, and hands over the eyes
2.tomorrow: you already speak a little Yiddish
2.howItsDone: On Friday before sunset, many Jewish homes light two Shabbat candles (some add one for each child); the one lighting circles their hands over the flames, covers their eyes and says the blessing, then greets the family with Shabbat shalom.

screen: `DAY TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the mezuzah, the words on the doorpost. Your line was take the words with you. Today, two small flames on a Friday.
screen: `TAKE THE WORDS WITH YOU.` → `DAY 2.`

segments.voice: Friday afternoon, and the clock is running. The oven's on, someone's still in the shower, a kid can't find their shoes. Then, at a minute printed on a calendar on the fridge, someone strikes a match and lights two candles. They circle their hands over the flames, cover their eyes, and whisper a blessing. When they look up, the week is over.
screen: `FRIDAY, THE CLOCK RUNNING.` → `TWO CANDLES.` → `HANDS OVER THE EYES.`

segments.voice: This is how Shabbat begins: the day of rest, from Friday sunset until the stars come out on Saturday night. Why sunset? In the Torah's first chapter, each day closes the same way: there was evening and there was morning. Evening comes first, so a day starts in the dark. And since lighting a fire is one of the kinds of work that stop on Shabbat, the candles go on while it's still light, in many towns eighteen minutes early, as a margin. Why two? The rest day is commanded twice, in two wordings: remember the day, and observe it. Zachor and shamor. One flame for each. Then the hands over the eyes. Usually you say a blessing and then do the thing. But once this blessing is said, Shabbat has begun, and no new fire can be lit. So people light first, cover their eyes, bless, and then look, as if the light were new. And why light at all? The rabbis said it's for shalom bayit, peace in the home: a light so the family can see each other's faces at dinner.
screen: `EVENING FIRST, THEN MORNING.` · `REMEMBER AND OBSERVE.` · `LIGHT, COVER, BLESS, LOOK.` · `PEACE IN THE HOME.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Look at the nearest light: a lamp, a window, even this screen. Breathe in. Close your eyes, the way people do after lighting. As you breathe out, open them slowly, as if the light were new.
The candles. Two flames before sunset on Friday: remember, and observe. Second word.

3.title: you already speak a little Yiddish
3.hook: mazel tov, oy vey, schlep: a whole language hiding in English
3.tomorrow: the plate that tells a story
3.howItsDone: Yiddish is still spoken in some Hasidic communities and is studied and sung widely; many Jews, religious or not, use Yiddish words every day, say mazel tov after good news, and call a decent person a mensch.

screen: `DAY THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the candles, two flames before sunset. Your line was light, then rest. Today, words you may have been saying for years.
screen: `LIGHT, THEN REST.` → `DAY 3.`

segments.voice: Mazel tov. Oy vey. Schlep, kvetch, chutzpah, nosh. Plenty of people say these without a second thought, Jewish or not. They aren't slang. They're Yiddish, a whole language with its own songs, newspapers and novels, and a lot of English speakers have been using a little of it all along.
screen: `MAZEL TOV. OY VEY. SCHLEP.` → `NOT SLANG.` → `A WHOLE LANGUAGE.`

segments.voice: Yiddish was the everyday language of Ashkenazi Jews in central and eastern Europe for centuries. It's built mostly from old German, with Hebrew and Slavic words mixed in, and it's written in Hebrew letters. Immigrants carried it to American cities, and English kept a handful. Schlep: to drag. Kvetch: to complain, at length. Nosh: a little snack. Chutzpah: nerve, rude or brave depending on who's telling it. Oy vey is short for oy vey iz mir: oh, woe is me. And mazel tov? Mazel comes from a Hebrew word for a star, and luck; tov means good. Good luck, word for word. But it isn't said before the exam. It's said after the good news: a birth, a wedding, a new job. It means: a good thing happened. Then there's the word worth keeping. In German, Mensch just means a person. In Yiddish, a mensch is a real human being: decent, honest, someone who does the right thing when nobody's checking. The great rabbi Hillel taught it long before Yiddish existed: where nobody is acting like a person should, try to be that person.
screen: `A LANGUAGE IN HEBREW LETTERS.` · `SCHLEP, KVETCH, NOSH.` · `MAZEL TOV — AFTER, NOT BEFORE.` · `A MENSCH — A REAL HUMAN BEING.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. First breath: someone you'd call a mensch. Second breath: one thing they did when nobody was checking. Third breath: let the word land on them, quietly, like a compliment they'll never hear.
Mensch. A real human being: decent, honest, there when it counts. Third word.
screen: `MENSCH — your 3rd word`.

segments.voice: Your line: be a mensch. Of everything Yiddish lent to English, that may be the best one. Day three, done.

4.title: the plate that tells a story
4.hook: a bone, an egg, parsley and horseradish: the Passover plate, and why the answer starts with we
4.howItsDone: On the first night of Passover (the first two, for many outside Israel), Jewish families hold a seder, reading the Haggadah around the table: the youngest asks the four questions, the story is told in the first person, and matzah, bitter herbs, charoset and a green vegetable in salt water are eaten as part of the telling.

screen: `DAY FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: mensch, a decent human being. Your line was be a mensch. Today, a plate where every food is part of a story.
screen: `BE A MENSCH.` → `DAY 4.`

segments.voice: A spring night, a long table, chairs borrowed from the neighbors. In the middle sits a plate with odd little things on it: a roasted bone, an egg, some parsley, horseradish, a brown sweet paste. Nobody's eating them yet. Then the youngest kid stands up, a little nervous, and asks: why is this night different from all other nights?
screen: `A BONE, AN EGG, PARSLEY.` → `THE YOUNGEST STANDS UP.` → `WHY IS THIS NIGHT DIFFERENT?`

segments.voice: Seder means order. Passover night follows a set order of steps, read from a little book called the Haggadah, which means the telling. The story it tells is the Exodus: slaves in Egypt, a stubborn king, ten plagues, and a night of leaving so rushed the bread had no time to rise. That's the matzah. The plate is the story laid out as food. Bitter herbs, often horseradish, for how bitter slavery was. Charoset, a sweet paste often made of apples, nuts and wine, looks like the mortar the slaves used for bricks. A green vegetable, often parsley, dipped in salt water, like tears. The roasted bone recalls the lamb of the first Passover; the egg, an offering brought on festivals long ago. You taste the story before anyone explains it. Then comes the surprise. The answer to the child's question doesn't start with once upon a time. It starts: we were slaves. We. The old rule is that in every generation, each person should see themselves as if they personally walked out of Egypt. Not a history lesson. A memory you're handed.
screen: `SEDER — ORDER.` · `THE BREAD THAT DIDN'T RISE.` · `THE STORY LAID OUT AS FOOD.` · `WE WERE SLAVES.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. First breath: something bitter from this year. Second breath: something sweet that came anyway. Third breath: hold the two together, the bitter and the sweet, the way the plate does.
Seder. Order: Passover night told step by step, with the story laid out on a plate. Fourth word.
screen: `SEDER — your 4th word`.

segments.voice: Your line: we were slaves. Not they. We. That one word carries the whole night. Day four.

story.title: the basket in the reeds
story.text: A king orders every newborn boy among the slaves thrown into the river. One mother hides her baby for three months, until she can't hide him any longer. She seals a basket with tar, lays him in it, and sets it among the reeds, while his older sister watches from a distance. The king's own daughter comes down to bathe, hears the baby crying, and takes pity on him. His sister steps forward, offers to find a nurse, and runs to bring back his mother. The princess names him Moses.

5.title: why the glass breaks
5.hook: one stomp, a crunch, and everyone shouts mazel tov: why break something at a wedding?
5.howItsDone: At the end of a Jewish wedding under the chuppah, a glass wrapped in cloth is broken underfoot, traditionally by the groom and at many weddings today by either partner or both, and the guests shout mazel tov.

screen: `DAY FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the seder, a story laid out as food. Your line was we were slaves. Today, the loudest second of a Jewish wedding.
screen: `WE WERE SLAVES.` → `DAY 5.`

segments.voice: The end of the ceremony. The couple stands under a canopy. Someone sets a glass, wrapped in a cloth, on the floor. One stomp, a crunch, and the whole room shouts mazel tov. Plenty of people have cheered for it without knowing why it happens. And there's more than one answer: families tell it different ways.
screen: `A GLASS IN A CLOTH.` → `ONE STOMP.` → `MAZEL TOV!`

segments.voice: Start with the canopy. It's called a chuppah: four poles and a cloth, open on every side, like the roof of a home that's just beginning. Then the glass. Its roots go back to rabbis in ancient Babylon who broke a precious cup at a wedding feast, on purpose, when the celebrating got out of hand. Later teachers tied the custom to Jerusalem, and the Temple that stood there, destroyed nearly two thousand years ago. An old psalm promises to keep Jerusalem above even your highest joy. So at the happiest moment, something breaks: a reminder that even on the best day, something in the world is still broken. Families add their own readings. Love is precious and breakable, so handle it with care. A glass, once broken, stays broken; the promise is meant to be just as permanent. In some old customs, the noise scared off bad luck. Traditionally the groom breaks it; at many weddings today, either partner does, or both together. More than one meaning can be true at once, and a Jewish wedding is happy to hold them all. Then comes the shout, the words you met two days ago: mazel tov.
screen: `THE CHUPPAH — OPEN ON EVERY SIDE.` · `A PRECIOUS CUP, BROKEN.` · `REMEMBER JERUSALEM.` · `MORE THAN ONE MEANING.`

6.title: not just a party
6.hook: a thirteen-year-old, an ancient scroll, then the DJ: which part is the real thing?
6.tomorrow: an argument for the sake of heaven
6.howItsDone: A Jewish boy becomes bar mitzvah at thirteen and a girl bat mitzvah at twelve in traditional law (thirteen in many communities); many mark it by being called up to read from the Torah, often chanting the week's portion and giving a short talk, followed by a festive meal, and some adults celebrate it later in life.

screen: `DAY SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the glass, broken right before the cheering. Your line was even in joy, remember. Today, a day many people remember for the DJ.
screen: `EVEN IN JOY, REMEMBER.` → `DAY 6.`

segments.voice: A thirteen-year-old in a suit that doesn't quite fit, or a dress picked out months ago, stands in front of everyone they know and chants from a handwritten scroll, in Hebrew they've practiced for a year. Then comes the party: the DJ, the candy bar, the chair lifted into the air. So which part was the real thing? Neither one, it turns out, makes it happen.
screen: `THIRTEEN, AND A SCROLL.` → `THEN THE DJ.` → `WHICH PART IS REAL?`

segments.voice: Bar mitzvah means son of the commandment. Bat mitzvah, daughter of the commandment. A mitzvah is one of the things the Torah asks a person to do, and in everyday talk it's also a good deed: that was a real mitzvah. Here's the twist. You don't have a bar or bat mitzvah. You become one. In traditional Jewish law it happens on its own, on a birthday: thirteen for boys, twelve for girls, and many communities mark both at thirteen. Ceremony or no ceremony, party or no party, the day comes. An old teaching lays out a life by ages: five for starting scripture, ten for the rabbis' teachings, thirteen for the commandments. Until then, the responsibility sat with your parents. From that birthday on, it's yours. So the ceremony isn't what makes it happen. It's the first time it's shown in public: called up to read from the Torah, often with a short talk about what that week's reading means to you. And the party? Celebrating a mitzvah with a festive meal is a tradition too. The DJ is newer. Some people take it up as adults, at thirty or sixty or eighty. There's no deadline.

story.title: the first girl to stand up
story.text: On a Saturday morning in March 1922, in a New York synagogue, a twelve-year-old girl stands up to do something no girl there has done before. Her father, the rabbi, has decided his daughter will mark her coming of age in public, just as boys do. After the regular service, she says the blessing and reads from that week's portion, in Hebrew and in English. She reads from a printed book, not the scroll, standing a careful distance from where the men read. Her name is Judith Kaplan, and hers is often called the first public bat mitzvah in America.

segments.voice: Open a page of the Talmud, the great library of the rabbis' discussions, and you'll find something you might not expect in a holy book: arguments. One rabbi says this. Another says no, that. Then a third weighs in. And very often the side that lost is written down too, and kept, for centuries. A holy book that saves its disagreements.
screen: `A PAGE OF THE TALMUD.` → `ONE SAYS THIS, ONE SAYS THAT.` → `THE LOSING SIDE, KEPT.`

segments.voice: Machloket means a disagreement. And there's a famous pair at the center of it: Hillel and Shammai, two great teachers about two thousand years ago, and the schools of students who followed them. You met Hillel on day three. The two schools argued for years, about prayer, about Shabbat, about how to live. Finally, the story goes, a voice from heaven settled it: both of these are the words of the living God. And the law follows Hillel. Wait. Both are right, but one wins? Why Hillel? Because, the story says, his students were kind and humble. They taught Shammai's view along with their own, and even taught Shammai's first. An old teaching names the difference between a good argument and a bad one. An argument for the sake of heaven will last, and its example is Hillel and Shammai. An argument to win, to beat someone, won't. Remember the slanted mezuzah from day one: an argument where nobody had to lose. So when Jews argue over a text, often out loud, in pairs, across a table, it isn't a lack of faith. It's how people learn.

story.title: the oven, the tree and the voice
story.text: A rabbi is losing an argument about whether a certain oven can be used, and he's sure he's right. If I'm right, he says, let this carob tree prove it, and the tree tears itself out of the ground. Let the stream prove it, and the water flows backward. Finally a voice from heaven announces that he's right. The other rabbis still won't budge: the Torah is not in heaven, one of them says; it was given to people to work out. Later, the story goes, God laughed and said: my children have won.
story.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 59b (the oven of Akhnai)
